Stage 3 · Grammar

Four ways to say you could do it

General ability, one occasion, and success after difficulty.

Read these four sentences from the study.
  • Everyone can learn to wait if they want to.
  • Only thirty per cent were able to resist temptation.
  • Some managed to wait a while before giving in.
  • Nearly all the children succeeded in waiting the full fifteen minutes.
Which of them tell you it was difficult?
Saying you could do something and saying you managed to do it are not the same claim.

English has several ways of expressing ability, and they are not simply stylistic alternatives. Can and could are modal verbs describing a general capacity. Be able to supplies the forms that modals structurally cannot take. Manage to and succeed in add something the others do not: the idea that the thing was difficult and was nevertheless achieved on a particular occasion.

The key distinction — and the one that separates B1 from A2 here — concerns the past. Could describes a skill that existed over a period of time: I could swim by the age of six. It does not describe one successful action on one occasion. For that, English requires was/were able to or managed to: He managed to free one hand. Saying Yesterday I could finish the report sounds wrong to a native ear because could reports a capacity, not an achievement.

Curiously, this restriction disappears in the negative. Couldn’t works for both a general inability and a single failed occasion: He couldn’t phone for help is perfectly correct. It also survives with verbs of perception and thinking — I could hear the river, I could see the path — even on one occasion.

The second structural point is that English permits only one modal per verb phrase. That is why will can and have could do not exist, and why be able to is indispensable: it is the only form that can follow another modal, sit in a perfect tense, or work as an infinitive. You’ll be able to…, I haven’t been able to…, I’d love to be able to…

Before you look at the table: the table below sets the four expressions against each other by what they claim — capacity, achievement, or difficulty overcome. Read that column before you look at the forms.
The four forms
FormWhat it saysFollowed byExample
can / can’tgeneral ability nowplain verbShe can swim. I can’t drive.
could / couldn’tgeneral ability in the pastplain verbHe could read at four.
be able toability in any tense — the only one that works after will, have, toto + verbThey were able to wait. You’ll be able to choose.
manage tosucceeded, and it was difficult — one occasionto + verbShe managed to wait fifteen minutes.
succeed insucceeded after effort — more formal-ingHe succeeded in saving the money.

The one rule people get wrong. For a single occasion in the past, use was/were able to or managed to, not could. Could is for general ability: He could swim as a child, but He managed to swim to the boat that night.

Negatives are different. Couldn’t is fine for a single occasion: I couldn’t open the door. The restriction only applies to the positive.

The form to memorise. succeed in + -ing, never succeed to do. And manage to + plain verb, never manage doing.

Where be able to is the only choice. After will, after have, and after to: You’ll be able to choose, I’ve been able to do it since Monday, I want to be able to cook.

Full grammar reference — ability — can, could, be able to, manage to, succeed in

What it is

English has several ways of saying that somebody has the ability to do something or that they achieved it. Can and could are modal verbs and cover general ability. Be able to supplies the forms that modals do not have. Manage to and succeed in add the idea that the thing was difficult and was nevertheless achieved on a particular occasion.

What it means, and what it does

The choice communicates more than ability. I could swim at five reports a general skill; I managed to swim to the boat reports a single hard-won success. Getting this wrong makes a real difference to meaning: He could pass the exam says he had the ability, while He managed to pass the exam says he actually did it, with difficulty.

When and why we use it

English has several ways of expressing ability, and they are not simply stylistic alternatives. Can and could are modal verbs describing a general capacity. Be able to supplies the forms that modals structurally cannot take. Manage to and succeed in add something the others do not: the idea that the thing was difficult and was nevertheless achieved on a particular occasion.

The key distinction — and the one that separates B1 from A2 here — concerns the past. Could describes a skill that existed over a period of time: I could swim by the age of six. It does not describe one successful action on one occasion. For that, English requires was/were able to or managed to: He managed to free one hand. Saying Yesterday I could finish the report sounds wrong to a native ear because could reports a capacity, not an achievement.

Curiously, this restriction disappears in the negative. Couldn’t works for both a general inability and a single failed occasion: He couldn’t phone for help is perfectly correct. It also survives with verbs of perception and thinking — I could hear the river, I could see the path — even on one occasion.

The second structural point is that English permits only one modal per verb phrase. That is why will can and have could do not exist, and why be able to is indispensable: it is the only form that can follow another modal, sit in a perfect tense, or work as an infinitive. You’ll be able to…, I haven’t been able to…, I’d love to be able to…

Typical situations

You will use these forms to describe skills and qualifications, to talk about what you achieved in a difficult situation, to explain what stopped you doing something, and to talk about what will be possible in future.

  • General ability now — can for a skill or possibility in the present.She can hold her breath for two minutes.
  • General ability in the past — could for a skill that lasted over a period.I could ride a bike by the age of six.
  • Ability in a form modals cannot take — be able to after another modal, in the perfect, or as an infinitive.I’d love to be able to speak Japanese. · She has been able to retrain.
  • A single difficult success in the past — managed to or was able to, not could.He managed to free one hand. · They were able to reach the shore.
  • Formal or written achievement — succeed in + -ing.If you succeed in turning your attention away, you may forget about it.
  • Inability on one occasion — couldn’t works for both general and single-occasion inability.He couldn’t phone for help.

How it differs from similar structures

could = had the ability · managed to / was able to = actually did it, once, with difficulty. He could open the window (he knew how) vs He managed to open the window (it was stuck, but he did).
can = ability or permission · be allowed to = permission only. Lesson 8 separates these.

How to build it

can / could: subject + can / could + base verb (no to, no -s)
be able to: subject + am / is / are / was / were / will be / have been + able to + base verb
manage to: subject + manage(d) to + base verb
succeed in: subject + succeed(ed) in + verb-ing
AffirmativeShe can wait. · He could swim. · They were able to escape. · I managed to finish.
NegativeShe can’t wait. · He couldn’t swim. · They weren’t able to escape. · I didn’t manage to finish.
QuestionCan she wait? · Could he swim? · Were they able to escape? · Did you manage to finish?
Short answersYes, she can. / No, he couldn’t. / Yes, they were. / No, I didn’t.
With another modalwill can → will be able to. You’ll be able to take the test again.
In the perfecthave could → have been able to. I haven’t been able to reach her.

Spelling and word order

  • Modals never take -s, -ing or -ed: she cans, canning, coulded do not exist.
  • Manage drops the -e before -ing: managing. Succeed keeps both es: succeeded, succeeding.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • can in a positive sentence is weak and almost swallowed: /kən/. can’t is long and stressed: /kɑːnt/ (British). The vowel length, not the final t, is what listeners hear.
  • could is also weak in fast speech (/kəd/) and is easily missed. Couldn’t is stressed.
  • In be able to the to is reduced to /tə/, so able to go sounds like ‘able t’go’.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The key restriction: use could for general past ability over a period, but was / were able to or managed to for a single successful action. I could swim (skill) but I was able to swim to the boat (one occasion). This restriction disappears in the negative: couldn’t is correct for both.
  • With verbs of perception and thinking — see, hear, feel, understand, remember — could is normal even for one occasion: I could hear the river.
  • Manage to always implies difficulty. I managed to eat breakfast sounds odd unless breakfast really was a struggle.
  • Succeed in takes -ing, never to: succeeded in finishing, not succeeded to finish. It is more formal than manage to.
  • Be able to is the only option after another modal or in a perfect or infinitive form, because English allows just one modal per verb phrase.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Yesterday I could finish the report. → Yesterday I managed to finish the report.A single past achievement takes managed to or was able to.
  • She cans wait fifteen minutes. → She can wait fifteen minutes.Modals take no -s.
  • I will can help you tomorrow. → I will be able to help you tomorrow.Two modals cannot follow each other.
  • He succeeded to resist the temptation. → He succeeded in resisting the temptation.Succeed in takes the -ing form.
  • Did you managed to wait? → Did you manage to wait?After did the verb returns to its base form.
  • I am able to swim since I was six. → I have been able to swim since I was six.Since requires a perfect form.

More examples in context

  • present skillSome children can wait fifteen minutes for a second marshmallow.
  • past skillAt that age I could already read music.
  • single successAfter three attempts she managed to beat her own record.
  • single success, neutralThe rescue team were able to reach him before dark.
  • formalThe researchers succeeded in showing a link between patience and success.
  • inabilityHe couldn’t resist — he ate it after four minutes.
  • perceptionI could hear the river below the trail.
  • after a modalWith practice you’ll be able to do it without thinking.
  • perfectI haven’t been able to concentrate all week.
  • questionDid any of them manage to resist the marshmallow?

A tip for remembering it

Ask yourself: skill, or single success? A skill that lasted over time takes could. One difficult thing that actually came off takes managed to or was able to. And whenever a modal is already in the sentence, or you need a perfect or an infinitive, switch to be able to.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Can / could + base verb; modals take no -s, -ing or -ed.
  2. Could = general past ability; managed to / was able to = one difficult success.
  3. Couldn’t covers both general and single-occasion inability.
  4. Use be able to after another modal, in the perfect, or as an infinitive.
  5. Succeed in + -ing; manage to + base verb.
  6. Could is fine for one occasion with see, hear, feel, understand, remember.

Stage 5 · Main input

The marshmallow test

The experiment, and what it really predicted.

Before you read: four-year-olds were offered one marshmallow now, or two if they could wait fifteen minutes.

What proportion of the children do you think managed to wait?

Decide first. Paragraph A gives you the answer.

The children who waited

A test with a marshmallow seemed to predict how children’s lives would turn out. Fifty years later, researchers are still arguing about what it really measured.

AThe experiment could not have been simpler. A researcher put a marshmallow on a plate in front of a four-year-old and made a promise. “If you can be patient and wait until I come back, you can have two.” Then he left the room. What happened next was filmed, and the films are still difficult to watch: children who could not resist covered their eyes, turned their backs, sang to themselves, and sat on their hands. Most of them gave in before the fifteen minutes were up.

BThe psychologist behind it, Walter Mischel, began this work at Stanford University around 1970. He was not really interested in marshmallows. He wanted to measure something much harder to see: whether a small child could hold on to a reward that was not there yet. The successful children were not the ones who stared at the plate and made an enormous effort. They were the ones who managed to turn their attention away from it — and if you succeed in doing that, Mischel argued, you may forget about the temptation altogether.

CYears later, his team went back to the same children, who were now teenagers. The results were striking. Those who had been able to wait longer had better exam results, coped better with stress, and were described by their parents as more socially confident. The study became one of the most famous experiments in psychology, and its conclusion spread far beyond the laboratory: teach children to wait, and you improve their lives.

DThen, in 2018, a team led by Tyler Watts repeated the study with a much larger and more varied group of children. They found something more complicated. Children who waited did tend to do better later — but once the researchers took the family’s income and education into account, most of the difference disappeared. A child from a secure home has good reasons to trust a promise. A child who has learned that promised things often do not arrive has good reasons to eat the marshmallow now.

EThis does not mean the original experiment was worthless. It was probably measuring two things at once: the ability to resist, and the experience that makes resisting seem sensible. In one version of the test, researchers deliberately broke a promise to one group of children before the marshmallow appeared. Those children waited, on average, about a third as long as the others. They had not become less patient. They had simply stopped believing the researcher.

FSo what should we take from it? Not that some children are born to succeed and others are not. Mischel himself always insisted that waiting is a technique rather than a personality: you can teach a child to look away, to think about something else, to make a plan. What the newer research adds is a second, less comfortable point. Before you can ask a child to wait for a reward, somebody has to make sure the reward actually comes.

Written for this course. Based on published accounts of Walter Mischel’s Stanford experiments (from 1970) and on Watts, Duncan and Quan, Psychological Science, 2018.
